children: A top regulatory officer at Nasdaq explains the company's concerns about how the agency is implementing tokenized securities.
By John Zecca
The tokenization of real-world assets, including equities, is quickly moving from a theoretical possibility to reality.

Despite the Clarity Act failing to pass the Senate this year, the Securities and Exchange Commission is moving full-steam ahead to tokenize stocks. In September, it issued a five-year "Innovation Exemption" for tokenized stocks to trade outside the established framework that governs U.S. stock trading.

Much of the conversation around the start of this massive evolution in markets has focused on how tokenization will benefit investors by making trading more accessible. Far less attention has been paid to what it can offer the companies whose shares are being tokenized.

Nasdaq recognizes that, if properly designed, tokenization can be a big positive for share issuers. Research estimates that the financial industry spends roughly $58 billion annually processing corporate actions like dividends and stock splits. Greater standardization, automation, and real-time processing can significantly reduce those costs. By embedding standardized data and automation directly into digital securities, tokenization can reduce reconciliation, streamline settlement and corporate actions, and improve how issuers communicate with shareholders.
But realizing those benefits depends on market structure as much as the technology.

Before the SEC launched the Innovation Exemption, a time and volume-limited pilot program for tokenized securities, Nasdaq advocated for a requirement that a venue provides issuers notice and an opt-out opportunity before the venue starts trading a tokenized version of the issuer's stock. We commend the Commission for moving tokenization forward — there are enormous potential benefits to be had.

But the framework as it's currently written raises concerns about whether those benefits can be fully realized. Based on those concerns, Nasdaq intends to opt its own stock out of Tokenized Securities Venues.
Here is why.

Any tokenization framework should do three things: preserve the rights associated with the underlying shares, maintain the principle that a tokenized stock remains a stock, and give issuers a meaningful voice in how their stock is tokenized. That principle carried markets from paper certificates to electronic records, and it should carry them into tokenization. Technology can change how a stock is represented to shareholders, but it doesn't change the underlying principles and protections that come with owning it.

Our greater concern, however, is that the Innovation Exemption allows tokenized securities to trade outside the government-regulated National Market System, which maintains a market data, reporting, and transparency framework that all stock trading must abide by.

If tokenized stocks don't have to adhere to the National Market System, fragmentation could occur. A single stock could be splintered into three, five, or seven tokenized versions, that the issuer never authorized — each in a different venue with its own price and liquidity. The National Market System, by contrast, allows liquidity to exist across multiple venues while connecting those venues through common infrastructure.

For issuers, that fragmentation will complicate price discovery, liquidity, shareholder engagement, and the delivery of a consistent ownership experience. It could also create new costs as they piece together liquidity and market information across disconnected venues and navigate different market rules. Without interoperability or fungibility, those costs could offset the efficiencies tokenization is meant to deliver.

Nasdaq has considered these concerns both as a market operator and as an issuer. We don't believe our stock should trade on venues that lack the trade reporting and market protections our investors expect. Different companies will reach different conclusions about those trade-offs. We support their right to make that choice for themselves.

Those who disagree with us might say that requiring tokenized venues to operate within the same core market framework as the rest of the National Market System defeats the purpose of tokenization — that parallel architectures are where experimentation happens, and that lower regulatory burdens are the price of innovation. There is an important role for experimentation, but the conditions that enable experimentation aren't necessarily the conditions that allow a market to scale.

We believe that tokenization can't reach its potential at scale if its benefits come at the cost of fragmented liquidity, uneven transparency, added costs and complexity, or a diminished shareholder experience. And if tokenization is to be truly transformative, it has to become part of the market, fully integrated rather than standing apart.
Our decision to opt out of tokenized securities venues reflects our view about how tokenization should scale up, not a hesitation about its potential benefits.

We also know that public companies are more than the securities that trade in their name. They have responsibilities to their shareholders, invest deeply in those relationships, and depend on markets that provide transparent price discovery, reliable liquidity and confidence in ownership. The question for tokenization is no longer simply what the technology can do. It is whether we can build a market in which its benefits reach investors and issuers at scale.
